newsitem.title: USA: Rudman named Pentagon adviser on Gulf ills.
newsitem.headline: Rudman named Pentagon adviser on Gulf ills.

text.p: Former New Hampshire Sen. Warren Rudman will become a special adviser to the Defence Department on an investigation into the health problems of Gulf War veterans, the Pentagon said on Thursday.
The department released a letter from Defence Secretary William Cohen thanking Rudman, a Republican who retired from the Senate in 1992, for accepting the post.

Rudman, respected by Democrats and Republicans for a tough and impartial approach to issues while he served in Congress, is currently vice chairman of President Bill Clinton's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board.
Tens of thousands of U.S. military Gulf War veterans have complained of physical and mental problems ranging from joint aches to memory loss, but no common cause of the complaints has been found.

Thursday's announcement came on the same day the Pentagon said Deputy Secretary John White, who now has senior responsibility for the Gulf illness investigation, will leave the Defence Department in June to return to private life.

The Pentagon and other agencies are looking into the possibility that some complaints could have resulted from the escape of Iraqi nerve gas when U.S. troops destroyed a chemical weapons dump in southern Iraq in 1991 just after the war ended.

The CIA recently said it had information ahead of the destruction that shells and rockets containing Sarin and possibly other agents were present at the Kamisiyah ammunition dump but that military officials were not warned.

The Pentagon is in the process of checking more than 15,000 troops who served in the 82nd Airborne Division and other units and who may have been within range of a cloud produced by the blasts which destroyed the dump.
Cohen, a Maine Republican, served in the Senate with Rudman. He left the Senate this year and was named by Clinton to replace Defence Secretary William Perry.

"You have answered your country's call many times -- as a soldier during the Korean War, as a senator and now as vice chairman of the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board," Cohen wrote to Rudman in a letter dated April 30.
"I am pleased that you have agreed to take on this job for the benefit of our soldiers and veterans."
